To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) Deep residual models can be trained to augment text-embedding methods to improve performance on retrieval tasks; (2) The best performing base embedding is the word2vec model, followed by the fastText, Glove, and finally the word2vec CBOW model; (3) The performance of all embeddings is improved with the addition of IDF weighting; (4) The performance of the best base embeddings can be improved by 14% on the question side, by augmenting them
the best text-embeddings for retrieval from a large knowledge base are learned using a neural network trained for this purpose.

(1) deep residual models are superior to shallow neural models for this task; (2) augmenting base embedding with neural models trained for this task yields significant performance gain; (3) the best base embedding is the concatenation of GloVe, ELMo and BERT.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a retrieval system that can find paragraphs that contain answers to a given question, and the results are promising
the following questions: (a) Can we improve the performance of a retrieval system using a neural network?
the following two aspects: (1) how to use neural networks to improve text embeddings for retrieval; (2) how to apply text embeddings for retrieval in open-domain question answering.

our proposed method is the best performing approach for this task.
our learned embeddings are able to improve the top-1 paragraph recall by 14% and 8% on the question and paragraph sides respectively.
the combination of a base embedding with a learned neural model for retrieval can significantly improve the performance of a retrieval system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of deep neural models for retrieval can yield significant gains in performance.

the combination of deep residual models trained specifically for the retrieval task and the use of the question-paragraph pairs in SQuAD dataset as training data is a promising approach for the task of open-domain question answering.
neural text embeddings trained for retrieval can be used to improve the performance of retrieval from large knowledge bases, and that the use of IDF weighting can be beneficial.
The main takeaway from our work is that
augmenting existing embeddings with a neural approach can be a viable approach to improve retrieval performance in a large-scale open-domain question answering system.
the use of deep residual neural models can improve the performance of text-embedding methods, which can in turn lead to better retrieval performance.
neural models specifically optimized for this task can be very effective at improving the retrieval performance of text embedding models.
